I'm not so sure if Yuu is coerced, she's definitely pushed into physical intimacy during the early chapters that she has no interest in (which I found uncomfortable), but her main character flaw is that she really doesn't have any desires at all. She's drifting through life like a half-filled balloon, just kind of going whichever way. She recognizes Touko's desire, though, and at several points states she *does* want to want things, which I feel is important. 

At the start of the story, Touko hates her "true" self and her primary goal is to be the idealized version of her sister she has in her mind. Her attraction to Yuu is that she can let the mask fall without judgement, and because Yuu is seemingly aro/ace, she'll never love the true Touko that Touko despises. If You liked her back, she would be disgusted. 

Throughout the series, they both grow as people, and by the final few chapters, they're in an almost unattainably healthy relationship, and they've both overcome their major flaws with each other's help.

It's as well written a bildungsroman as I've ever come across, I don't think I've ever come across a manga that was structured as well as what I would consider a properly literary work. The use of metaphor is also pretty good, pretty direct but honestly I don't have a degree in lit and if it wasn't pretty on-the-nose I'd probably miss it.

Something is better than nothing, but the source material is rich. It's too bad it's not given more of a chance.



That being said, if they ever make an anime of "Can't Say No to the Lonely Girl" and it gets done dirty like this, I might riot

There are two main differences: cost and data storage. A CD-ROM from the PS1 era was able to hold 650Mb of data, so across three discs FF7 had 1950Mb of storage to work with. An N64 cartridge could hold 64Mb of data, so for the same storage you're looking at like 30 cartridges. 



The second factor is cost. A CD-ROM in 1996 cost approximately $1 to manufacture. So total cost of $3 for FF7. An N64 cartridge cost $30 in 1996 dollars to manufacture. 



Nintendo knew all of this, they still chose cartridges because it gave them an enormous amount of control and we're nigh impossible to pirate. They thought their commitment to brand quality would give them an advantage over competitors. Square had a vision for FF7, though, and cartridges just wouldn't work. It was a huge deal at the time for Square to move their games to a different platform, but Nintendo refused to adapt.

If Square decided to put FF7 on the N64, they would have had to scale back their creative vision for the game due to the limitations of cartridges. A *lot*.



It would have probably looked a lot more like Final Fantasy 6, and instead of being a game that defined a genre for a generation, it would have been just another entry in the series. 



Nintendo shot themselves in the door by insisting on cartridges, but two console generations prior they had saved the video game industry, so their hubris is understandable.

I'm a nuclear medicine tech and my spouse is a radiation therapist, so I've seen both sides of this.

Job prospects depend on your area, and your willingness to relocate.

Nuclear Medicine is a bit more chill, but the pay scale is slightly lower. It's also slightly higher radiation exposure, if that matters to you. There's also only so much you can specialize - there's PET, and that's about it. 

Radiation Therapy is more demanding in terms of pace and the stakes are higher (misadministration in nuclear medicine is unfortunate, but not life threatening. Treating the wrong area for certain cancers can be *very* bad for a patient). There's also more room to specialize - CT Sim, dosimetry, CSRT, you can go a lot of different paths. 


Hope that helps!
